sections.heading: Being honest about how I have prayed
sections.text: God of grace, I have just prayed, and I know how weak my praying has been. My heart has been cold. My attention has wandered. I have spoken to you without the love, urgency, and honesty you deserve. Even my prayers need your mercy.
theological_themes: Honest confession that even sincere religious acts can be mixed with sin, weakness, and spiritual dullness.
Dependence on God’s grace not only for obvious failures but also for failures within prayer itself.

scripture_references.connection: Paul acknowledges that believers often do not know how to pray as they ought, and that God graciously helps them in that weakness. This supports the prayer’s honest admission that our praying is often poor and dependent on divine mercy.
David teaches that God receives a broken and contrite heart, not polished religious performance. This grounds the posture of confessing the poverty of one’s own prayers before God.

sections.heading: Resting my hope on Jesus, not on my praying
sections.text: If my confidence had to rest on the quality of my prayers, I would have no hope. But my hope is not in how well I speak. My hope is in Jesus. Let his worth cover what is weak and stained in me, and make even my poor prayers acceptable to you.
theological_themes: Christ’s merit, not the believer’s performance, is the ground of acceptance before God.
Prayer is received because of Jesus’ priestly work and righteousness, not because it is impressive in itself.

scripture_references.connection: Because Jesus is the great High Priest, believers are invited to come near to God’s throne for mercy and grace. The confidence is located in Christ’s priesthood, not in the strength or beauty of the believer’s prayer.
Peter says spiritual offerings are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. That directly supports the idea that even our worship and prayer need Christ to make them acceptable.

sections.heading: Asking for deeper repentance and stronger faith
sections.text: Make my sorrow over sin deeper and truer. Strengthen my faith in the blood of Jesus, which cleanses every sin. Teach me to walk close to my Redeemer with love, not with distance or mere duty. Break my heart over sin, and also break sin’s hold on my heart. Do not let me excuse myself quickly. Let me take my sin as seriously as it deserves, even while I trust that you are quicker to forgive than I am to come clean.
theological_themes: True repentance includes grief over sin and a real turning from it.
Faith rests in Christ’s cleansing blood while refusing to treat sin lightly.
God’s readiness to forgive does not minimize sin; it makes honest repentance possible.

scripture_references.connection: John joins the cleansing power of Jesus’ blood with honest confession of sin. This fits the prayer’s request for both stronger faith in Christ’s cleansing and a truthful dealing with sin before God.
Paul distinguishes godly grief, which leads to repentance, from worldly grief. The prayer asks for sorrow that actually turns the heart from sin rather than merely feeling bad about it.

sections.heading: Letting grace humble me instead of making me casual
sections.text: As I look at the greatness of your grace, humble me. Let your mercy bring me low in the right way—not into despair, but into honest shame over what my sin has cost. Since you have made peace with me through Christ, keep me from pride, carelessness, or self-congratulation. Let forgiveness make me more tender, more watchful, and more grateful.
theological_themes: Peace with God through Christ deepens repentance and gratitude rather than making sin seem small.
The forgiven believer remains sober about sin while secure in God’s mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers have peace with God through Jesus Christ and stand in grace. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God is reconciled to the believer while also showing that this peace is a gift, not a ground for pride.
God’s kindness is meant to lead people to repentance. This grounds the prayer’s desire that grace would humble and change the heart rather than make it careless.

sections.heading: Receiving Christ’s blessing over every part of my life
sections.text: Lord Jesus, my great High Priest, pour out the grace I need today. Bless what I take up and what I leave undone. Bless the thoughts in my mind, the words that come from my mouth, the paths my feet take, and the work my hands do. You lived to bless, died to bless, rose to bless, ascended to bless, took your throne to bless, and even now you reign and intercede for your people. So make my desires sincere, my prayers earnest, and my love warm and steady. Amen.
theological_themes: Christ’s ongoing priestly reign supplies grace for daily obedience.
The believer needs God’s blessing over thoughts, speech, choices, and actions.
Jesus’ whole saving work—life, death, resurrection, ascension, reign, and intercession—is for the good of his people.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents the risen Christ as the one who always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him. This supports the prayer’s confidence that Jesus continues to bless and help his people now.
Paul connects Christ’s death, resurrection, exaltation, and intercession. This closely matches the prayer’s movement from what Christ has done to what he continues to do for believers.
Paul calls believers to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. This grounds the prayer’s request that thoughts, words, steps, and deeds all come under Christ’s blessing and lordship.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The line asking to be “as slow to forgive myself as thou art ready to forgive me” could be misunderstood today as encouraging ongoing self-condemnation. I rendered it as taking sin seriously while still trusting God’s readiness to forgive, to preserve the Puritan concern for repentance without contradicting the gospel’s assurance.

The phrase “now thou art pacified towards me” reflects the doctrine of propitiation or God’s wrath being satisfied through Christ. I expressed this as God making peace through Christ, retaining the substance while avoiding wording that could sound as if God were emotionally appeased apart from the atonement.
significant_interpretive_choices: “The worth of Jesus perfumes my feeble breathings” was interpreted as Christ’s merit making weak prayers acceptable to God, not as the believer’s prayers becoming inherently worthy.
“Broken for sin and unto sin” was rendered as being broken over sin and having sin’s hold broken, since the original phrase suggests both grief for sin and a decisive turning against it.

The repeated sequence of Christ living, dying, rising, ascending, enthroned, and reigning “to bless” was kept as a summary of Christ’s whole saving work and ongoing priestly ministry, rather than reduced to a general statement that Jesus helps believers.
